items.prompt: Dana could have sent one Slack message asking all three teams to fix their retry logic. Based on L1, why does that message alone reliably fail to produce the fix?
choices: Because Slack messages are, in general, technically considered inferior to email for this kind of request
Because it has no owner, no deadline, and no artifact — it asks teams to do unscheduled work outside their own priorities
Because engineers, as a rule, ignore all requests coming from anyone who isn't their direct manager
Because retry logic is, in general, simply too complex a topic to explain inside a single chat message
items.explanation: The message can be technically correct and still change nothing, because nothing in it turns 'true' into someone's scheduled Tuesday. No owner, no deadline, no artifact anyone can point back to — that gap, not the message's accuracy, is what stalls it.
items.reference:
💬 Message

Correct, but no owner, deadline, or artifact

📄 PR + RFC

Owner, deadline, and a citable artifact

Why: being right doesn't get anything scheduled by itself.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'the bug is real, so telling people about it should be enough.' What's the flaw in that reasoning, per the unit's opening scenario?
choices: Being real doesn't automatically get scheduled — the message has no owner, deadline, or artifact turning it into someone's actual work
The bug, as it turns out, wasn't actually real at all; Dana was simply mistaken about it existing
Telling people about a bug is, per this reasoning, always sufficient on its own once the bug is confirmed
The teams, in this scenario, would most likely have fixed it eventually without any message being sent at all
items.explanation: Reality of the bug and the mechanism for acting on it are two different things. The message supplies the first; it's the working PR, the RFC, and the review nudges that supply the second.
items.reference:
💬 Message

Correct, but no owner, deadline, or artifact

📄 PR + RFC

Owner, deadline, and a citable artifact

Why: being right doesn't get anything scheduled by itself.

items.prompt: Which of the following is missing from 'hey, everyone's retry logic should check whether an error is retryable' that a working PR plus an RFC supplies?
choices: Technical correctness — the message itself, as written, is simply factually wrong about the bug
An owner, a deadline, and a concrete artifact people can act on and reference later
Nothing at all — per this reasoning the message alone is just as effective as a full PR and RFC
A manager's formal written sign-off, which the message alone was apparently missing
items.explanation: The message and the PR/RFC can carry the identical technical claim. What differs is whether anyone can act on it without reconstructing the whole argument from memory — that's the artifact's job.
items.reference:
💬 Message

Correct, but no owner, deadline, or artifact

📄 PR + RFC

Owner, deadline, and a citable artifact

Why: being right doesn't get anything scheduled by itself.

choices: A rare edge case that, according to this unit, mostly doesn't come up in day-to-day staff work
The normal condition — most staff-level impact happens without a reporting line to lean on
Something that, per this unit, only ever applies specifically to engineering managers, not ICs
A sign, according to this reasoning, that the org chart itself is fundamentally broken
items.explanation: The unit is explicit that this is the actual job description at that level, not a workaround for an unusual gap — a staff engineer whose influence stops at their direct reports has a much smaller radius than the title implies.
items.reference: Why: most staff-level technical direction is set through people who don't report to the person setting it.

items.prompt: Why does the unit treat 'no authority over the other teams' as Dana's normal starting position rather than an unusual obstacle?

Because Dana's particular situation was, per this framing, a rare exception to how the org usually works

items.reference: Why: most staff-level technical direction is set through people who don't report to the person setting it.

items.prompt: What's the actual proof, in this unit's model, that Dana's influence worked?
choices: The RFC itself being formally approved by every single person who read through it
All three teams' code actually adopting the shared library
Dana's own manager specifically praising the effort during a performance review
The original Slack thread about the bug simply getting a large number of replies
items.explanation: Adoption in real code is the outcome that counts. Approval, praise, or a lively thread can all happen without a single line of code ever changing.
items.reference: Why: the only evidence influence worked is that the code changed, not that people said nice things about the idea.

items.prompt: Why is 'the RFC got a lot of positive comments' not, by itself, evidence that Dana's push succeeded?
choices: Positive comments don't guarantee anyone changed their code — adoption in the codebase is the actual evidence
Comments left on RFCs are, as a general rule, usually dishonest or performative rather than genuine
RFCs, in this org, are formally graded on a rubric, while comments left on them simply aren't
It is, in fact, treated as fully sufficient evidence on its own according to this unit's model
items.explanation: Agreement in a comment thread is not the same event as a merged PR that actually replaces the old retry loop — only the second one is the outcome the unit is tracking.
items.reference: Why: the only evidence influence worked is that the code changed, not that people said nice things about the idea.

items.prompt: Six weeks after Dana started, what specifically confirms the push worked?
choices: Three teams' codebases now use one shared, tested retry library
Dana, as it turned out, received a formal promotion specifically for this effort
The original bug reports were, in the end, simply closed out as won't-fix by the teams
A leadership team sent out a company-wide announcement celebrating the whole effort
items.explanation: The unit's own measure of success is concrete and code-level: all three teams' actual implementations converged on one shared, working library.
items.reference: Why: the only evidence influence worked is that the code changed, not that people said nice things about the idea.

items.prompt: Why did Dana ship the working with_retry() fix in payments before writing the RFC?
choices: Writing real code is, as a general rule, always a strict prerequisite before writing any documentation at all
A working, tested implementation answers design questions concretely instead of leaving them open to hypothetical debate
Payments' own team lead, in this scenario, formally required that order before anything else could proceed
RFCs, as a technical matter, simply cannot reference or link to code that doesn't yet exist
items.explanation: Code-first turns 'here's an idea, what do you think' into 'here's a working implementation, here's why the other teams should adopt it' — a much cheaper thing for a reader to evaluate than an untested proposal.
items.reference:
🛠️ Code first — design questions resolved by what the code needed
📝 Argument first — same questions debated hypothetically, indefinitely

items.prompt: What does a merged PR with tests prove that an argument for the same fix, however well-reasoned, does not?
choices: That the idea survives contact with real code and real edge cases, not just abstract reasoning
That the author of the PR is, by definition, more senior than everyone currently reviewing it
That absolutely no one will ever raise any objection to it once it has merged
That it, from that point on, requires no further review at all from anyone on the team
items.explanation: An argument can be debated forever in the abstract; a merged, tested PR has already survived contact with real production behavior, which answers most of those hypothetical objections by existing.
items.reference:
🛠️ Code first — design questions resolved by what the code needed
📝 Argument first — same questions debated hypothetically, indefinitely

items.prompt: A colleague says the RFC should have come first so all three teams could weigh in on the design before any code existed. What does L2's Checkpoint conclude?
choices: Code-first was clearly wrong in this case and the RFC should always come first, no exceptions ever

For a fix Dana was already confident in, code-first resolved design questions with what the code actually needed, rather than hypothetical debate — though gathering input first is right when the design is genuinely still open
It genuinely doesn't matter at all which one comes first in any situation like this
RFCs, according to this conclusion, should essentially never be written for any decision at all
items.explanation: The unit isn't claiming code-first is universally correct — it's the right default when the proposer already has strong conviction and context, and the order inverts when the design space is genuinely still open (see L3).
items.reference:
🛠️ Code first — design questions resolved by what the code needed
📝 Argument first — same questions debated hypothetically, indefinitely

items.prompt: What does a short written RFC do that a live Slack thread structurally cannot?
choices: Convince every single reader noticeably faster than an equivalent live conversation would
Serve as a stable artifact people can reference and act on weeks later, instead of scattering across a thread
Guarantee, simply by existing, that everyone involved ends up genuinely agreeing with it
Fully replace the need for there to be any working code behind the proposal at all
items.explanation: A thread convinces only the people currently reading it and is buried within days; the RFC is a stable reference point a fourth team can catch up on without anyone re-explaining it from scratch.
items.reference:
💬 Thread — convinces readers-in-the-moment, then disappears
📄 RFC — a stable, citable reference weeks later

items.prompt: Why does the unit favor a short, under-two-page RFC over a comprehensive 15-page design doc?
choices: Short documents are, as a general rule, automatically considered more technically correct than long ones
A short document people actually finish reading does more work than a long one that goes unread
Writing long documents is, at this particular company, explicitly against stated team policy
Document length, per this reasoning, has essentially no effect on whether anyone actually reads it
items.explanation: The RFC's job is to be a stable reference point people actually read and can point back to, not to be exhaustive — comprehensiveness that goes unread accomplishes nothing.
items.reference:
💬 Thread — convinces readers-in-the-moment, then disappears
📄 RFC — a stable, citable reference weeks later

items.prompt: What three things did Dana's RFC do that a conversation alone doesn't?
choices: Named the problem with evidence, presented a concrete solution, and opened an explicit objection window with a deadline
Assigned direct blame to the two teams running buggy retry logic and escalated the matter to management
Summarized, in full, every single team's entire backlog of planned work for the quarter
Fully replaced the need for any future code review to ever happen again on this specific topic
items.explanation: Those three elements — evidence-backed problem, concrete proposed solution, and a bounded window for objections — are exactly what let the RFC end in a recorded decision instead of an open-ended discussion.
items.reference:
💬 Thread — convinces readers-in-the-moment, then disappears
📄 RFC — a stable, citable reference weeks later

items.prompt: Why did Dana's review comment pointing at the shared library work better than a team-wide announcement asking everyone to migrate?

Review comments are, under this team's policy, formally mandatory to act on within a fixed time window
Team-wide announcements are, as a rule, always ignored by engineers regardless of their specific timing
The review comment, in this case, happened to come from someone holding formal authority over the author

🔍 Review comment — lands while the code is already open

items.prompt: What's the main weakness of a team-wide announcement asking everyone to adopt a new pattern 'when relevant'?
choices: It's, in this case, simply visible to too many people across the organization all at once
It asks people to remember a request at some unscheduled future point, which tends to quietly never happen
Announcements are, as a technical matter, simply incapable of containing a link to real code
It requires, under this team's process, formal management sign-off before it can even be sent out
items.explanation: Deferred, unscheduled work is exactly the failure mode L1 identified in 'just tell people' — an announcement has the same structural gap as a Slack message: no moment that turns it into someone's actual work.
items.reference:
📣 Announcement — asks people to remember it later
🔍 Review comment — lands while the code is already open

items.prompt: L2 asks which of the four channels, if missing, would make the other three fail even when each is individually well-executed. What's the answer?
choices: Code — without working code existing, nothing else at all in the four-channel sequence really matters
Relationships — a perfectly-written RFC from someone without a track record competes for attention it won't win

Review — none of the other three channels, per this reasoning, depend on it in any real way

choices: Because trust is what determines whether a team lead spends limited attention reading the RFC at all
Because relationships, in this unit's model, are treated as entirely unrelated to whether code ends up adopted
Because building relationships is, at this org, simply a formal HR requirement unrelated to the actual outcome
Because having strong relationships, per this reasoning, replaces the need for a real working implementation

items.reference: Why: trust is the filter readers use to decide whose document gets attention first.

items.prompt: Per L2's leverage-point chart, which team is the highest-leverage place for Dana to spend limited review and relationship time?
choices: The specific team that already had a mostly-correct implementation of the retry logic in place
The team with the worst version of the bug and the most on-call pain from it

The team that, among the three, has the single largest number of engineers on its roster

items.reference: Why: a fixed amount of time buys the most adoption where the pain is already the most acute.

items.prompt: What two factors does L2 name as making a team or PR 'high leverage' for spending Dana's limited time?
choices: Team size overall, and the specific seniority level held by that team's tech lead
How bad that team's version of the bug is, and how much weight that reviewer's endorsement carries with their own team

Whether the team in question happens to use the exact same programming language as payments does

items.prompt: In with_retry(), what happens when the response status is 400?
choices: It retries the request up to max_attempts times
It returns immediately on the first attempt without retrying
It raises a NonRetryableError exception
It waits indefinitely for a different response
items.explanation: 400 isn't in retryable_statuses, so the function returns the response right away on the first attempt — retrying a request that's guaranteed to fail again wastes time and load for zero chance of success.
items.reference:
if response.status_code not in config.retryable_statuses:
    return response  # never retried

Why: with_retry() only retries statuses that could plausibly succeed on a second try.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of adding jitter (random.uniform(0, delay * 0.25)) to the backoff delay in with_retry()?
choices: To deliberately make the unit's own automated test suite flaky and unreliable on purpose
So a burst of callers retrying at once doesn't re-synchronize into another spike against the downstream service
To uniformly slow down every single outgoing request, regardless of whether that request actually failed
It has, as it turns out, no real functional purpose at all — it's purely decorative, cosmetic randomness
items.explanation: Without jitter, many callers that failed at the same moment would all retry at the same delay and hit the downstream service in a synchronized spike again — jitter spreads those retries out.
items.reference:
if response.status_code not in config.retryable_statuses:
    return response  # never retried

Why: with_retry() only retries statuses that could plausibly succeed on a second try.

items.prompt: Which specific test in the unit's code would have caught both teams' original buggy retry implementations before they shipped?
choices: test_success_stops_retrying_early
test_retryable_status_retries_up_to_max_attempts
test_non_retryable_status_returns_on_first_attempt
None of the tests would have caught the bug
items.explanation: That test asserts a 400 is returned after exactly one call — a retry-everything implementation would fail it immediately, which is precisely the bug the unit opened with.
items.reference:
if response.status_code not in config.retryable_statuses:
    return response  # never retried

Why: with_retry() only retries statuses that could plausibly succeed on a second try.

items.prompt: When Owen raises a real, specific objection about idempotency, which of Dana's three options does she actually take?
choices: Argue the point away and insist the library is close enough as-is
Quietly drop search-indexing from the rollout and move on
Treat the objection as a real design input and extend the library together with Owen
Escalate to a shared manager to overrule Owen's objection
items.explanation: Dana pairs with Owen and extends the library with an idempotency_key parameter — treating a correct objection as a genuine improvement rather than an obstacle to argue past.
items.reference:
❌ Argue it away — burns trust
❌ Drop the team — leaves the bug unfixed there
✅ Extend the library together — costs a week, produces a better library

items.prompt: Why does arguing Owen's objection away, even if Dana technically 'wins' the argument, cost more than it first appears to?
choices: It burns the trust that made notifications' fast, low-friction adoption possible in the first place
Winning an argument like that, as a general rule, always takes strictly longer than a pairing session would
Doing so would, in this scenario, violate an explicit rule that was stated directly in the RFC itself
It has, in this telling, essentially no real cost at all beyond simply looking bad in the moment
items.explanation: Relationships (Channel 4) are what got the RFC read quickly in the first place — spending that trust to win an argument against a correct technical objection erodes the exact asset the rest of the rollout depends on.
items.reference:
❌ Argue it away — burns trust
❌ Drop the team — leaves the bug unfixed there
✅ Extend the library together — costs a week, produces a better library

items.prompt: What did Dana and Owen actually add to the shared library to resolve the objection?
choices: A hard-coded retry limit that applies specifically and only to search-indexing's own code path
An optional idempotency_key parameter that lets a downstream service detect and skip duplicate side effects
An entirely separate, unrelated library built from scratch just for search-indexing's own use
A blanket rule that simply disables retries for search-indexing's requests entirely going forward
items.explanation: The optional idempotency_key parameter layers a new guarantee on top of the existing non-retryable-status check, without touching the behavior payments already depended on.
items.reference:
❌ Argue it away — burns trust
❌ Drop the team — leaves the bug unfixed there
✅ Extend the library together — costs a week, produces a better library

items.prompt: Why did half a day of pairing resolve Owen's objection faster than a written back-and-forth in the RFC's comments would have?
choices: Pairing let Dana ask follow-up questions in real time and see the actual duplicate-detection hook, instead of several slow async rounds
Written review comments are, as a technical matter, simply incapable of being used for real design discussion
Pairing sessions, as a rule, always get scheduled faster than written review comments ever get answered
Owen, as it happens, only ever responds to synchronous requests and never to anything written down
items.explanation: The missing piece was a detail about search-indexing's downstream service that async comments would have taken multiple slow round-trips to extract — pairing got it in one real-time conversation.
items.reference: Why: real-time follow-up questions collapse several async round-trips into one conversation.

items.prompt: What did Dana not yet know before pairing with Owen, that made a purely written reply insufficient on its own?
choices: The exact mechanism by which search-indexing's downstream service could detect a duplicate
Owen's job title within the search-indexing team
Whether search-indexing's codebase was written in Python
The existence of the original retry bug
items.explanation: That specific mechanism was the missing context — once Dana saw it directly, the idempotency_key design followed naturally, which is exactly what a several-round async exchange would have been slower to surface.
items.reference: Why: real-time follow-up questions collapse several async round-trips into one conversation.

items.prompt: What property of a decision makes gathering input before building the better order, even for someone with Dana's credibility?
choices: When the proposer, in this case Dana, already has a strong, fully-tested fix sitting in hand
When multiple genuinely open directions exist and the people affected have context the proposer lacks
When the decision at hand happens to be small in scope and easily reversible either way
When the other team involved simply happens to be unresponsive to messages sent their way
items.explanation: Code-first assumes the proposer already has enough conviction and context to build something worth reacting to — when that's not true, building first risks sinking real effort into a direction a conversation would have redirected.
items.reference:
🛠️ Strong evidence, clear direction → code first
❓ Genuinely open, others have context → input first

items.prompt: Which part of the search-indexing story is closer to 'gather input first,' rather than the code-first default established earlier in the unit?
choices: Payments' own original with_retry() fix, which Dana wrote and tested before anything else
The RFC document itself, which Dana wrote after the payments fix was already working
Pairing with Owen to learn his team's constraint before writing the idempotency_key code
Notifications' fast, low-friction adoption of the shared library back in week 2
items.explanation: Rather than guessing at a design and presenting another finished PR, Dana gathered Owen's actual constraint first — a small, deliberate inversion of the code-first default for this one piece.
items.reference:
🛠️ Strong evidence, clear direction → code first
❓ Genuinely open, others have context → input first

items.prompt: If a decision has one clear best answer and the proposer already has strong evidence for it, which order does L3 recommend?
choices: Gather input from everyone first, then build
Build first, then write it up — the same code-first default from L2
Skip both code and writing, and just announce the decision
Escalate immediately to a decision-maker without building or writing anything
items.explanation: The inversion only applies when the design space is genuinely open — when the proposer already has strong conviction and evidence, code-first remains the default, as established in L2 and reaffirmed here.
items.reference:
🛠️ Strong evidence, clear direction → code first
❓ Genuinely open, others have context → input first

items.prompt: Notifications adopted the shared library in week 2 with almost no discussion, while search-indexing pushed back in week 4. What actually explains the difference?
choices: Notifications' team lead was, in this telling, simply less experienced overall than Owen happened to be
Notifications' retry bug had the same shape as payments' and mapped over directly — search-indexing had a genuinely different failure mode (idempotency) layered on top
Dana, in this case, spent noticeably and deliberately less effort convincing search-indexing than she spent on notifications
The RFC document itself was, as it turned out, worded quite differently depending on which of the two teams read it
items.explanation: The variable wasn't the pitch or the code quality — it was whether the underlying problem matched. Notifications' bug mapped over cleanly; search-indexing's had an extra real constraint the library didn't yet cover.
items.reference: Why: a fix that fully solves one team's problem can be a partial solution for another with a different failure mode.

items.prompt: What's the mistake in treating every 'no' from a team as resistance to be overcome rather than checked?
choices: There is no mistake — every 'no' should always be treated as resistance to push through
It risks missing a genuine gap in the proposal, like Owen's real idempotency concern, instead of engaging with it
It's always faster in every case to simply escalate past a 'no'
Teams never have legitimate technical reasons to decline a proposal
items.explanation: Owen's objection was correct, not obstruction — treating it as resistance to be overcome rather than a real design input would have missed the actual gap in the library and cost the trust that made the rest of the rollout work.
items.reference: Why: a fix that fully solves one team's problem can be a partial solution for another with a different failure mode.

items.prompt: The unit's closing question raises a version of Owen's objection that's really about status ('my team's two sprints of work look wasted') rather than a technical concern. Based on the unit's model, which channel is best suited to that kind of objection?
choices: Writing yet another, even more detailed RFC section explaining the underlying technical trade-offs again
Adding more inline code comments explaining in detail why the shared library's design is correct
Relationships — a status concern needs to be addressed as a people/trust issue, not resolved with more technical artifacts
Escalating the matter immediately to a shared manager to have them settle it from above
items.explanation: A status objection dressed as a technical one won't be resolved by more code or more writing, because the actual concern isn't technical — it calls for the relationship channel: acknowledging the team's prior work directly, not out-arguing a proxy complaint.
items.reference: Why: a status concern dressed as a technical one needs a people-channel response, not another technical artifact.
